passages.t: Solomon made king, and the Levites counted
passages.happening:
‘When David was old and full of years, he installed his son Solomon as king over Israel’ (verse 1). He gathers the leaders, the priests and the Levites. The Levites aged thirty and over number 38,000 (verse 3): 24,000 to oversee the work of the house of the LORD, 6,000 officers and judges, 4,000 gatekeepers and 4,000 to praise the LORD with instruments (verses 4-5).

David divides them by the three sons of Levi, Gershon, Kohath and Merari, and the heads of their families are named (verses 6-23). Of Kohath's line, ‘Aaron and his descendants were set apart forever to consecrate the most holy things’ (verse 13), while ‘As for Moses the man of God, his sons were named among the tribe of Levi’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 22 gathered materials; this chapter and the next four gather people. Chapters 23 to 27 set out the Levites, the priests, the musicians, the gatekeepers and treasurers, and the officers of the kingdom. The lists are short on story, and they are meant to be. They gave the Chronicler's first readers their family trees and their place in the worship of the rebuilt temple. Who to notice: Aaron's line, set apart as priests, and Moses' sons, counted among the ordinary Levites.

The Levites were the tribe set apart in the law to serve the sanctuary. Within Levi, Aaron's descendants were the priests who offered sacrifice, and the rest assisted them. In the wilderness the three Levite clans carried the tabernacle: Kohath the holy objects, Gershon the curtains, Merari the frames. The family list here follows the same three lines. That Moses' descendants gained no priestly rank is worth noticing: the greatest figure of Israel's past passed no hereditary privilege to his sons. When Eleazar left only daughters, they married their cousins, keeping the family's line and duties within the clan, as in the case of Zelophehad's daughters in Numbers.

Verse 1 sums up Solomon's accession in one sentence. First Kings 1 tells it at length, with the aged David, his son Adonijah's bid for the throne, and Solomon anointed in haste. Chronicles passes over the struggle; chapters 28 and 29 will tell a public, orderly handing over. The two accounts tell the same succession for different purposes.
passages.later: First Kings begins, ‘Now King David was old and well along in years, and though they covered him with blankets, he could not keep warm’ (1 Kings 1:1), and the story of the succession follows.
passages.asks: Moses' sons were counted among the ordinary Levites. Ask whether you expect a place because of whose child you are. And ask what work in God's house you would do gladly if no one counted it as rank.

passages.t: From carrying the tent to serving the house
passages.happening:
The Levites are counted from twenty years old (verse 24). David had said, “The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to His people and has come to dwell in Jerusalem forever” (verse 25), so the Levites no longer need to carry the tabernacle (verse 26).

Their work now is to assist Aaron's descendants: the courts and chambers, the purifying of holy things, the showbread, the flour, the baking and all measures of quantity and size (verses 28-29). ‘They were also to stand every morning to give thanks and praise to the LORD, and likewise in the evening’ (verse 30), and serve at the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The key is David's word in verse 25. God has given his people rest, nuach, and has come to dwell, shakan, in Jerusalem. A God who dwells in one place no longer needs to be carried, so those who carried him are reassigned to serve and to praise. The word for dwell is related to the word for the tabernacle, and later Jewish tradition drew from it the term Shekinah for God's dwelling presence.

The age of service differs in the sources. Numbers counts Levites from thirty to fifty in one place and from twenty-five in another; this chapter counts from thirty in verse 3 and from twenty in verses 24 and 27, as David's final instructions; and Ezra has Levites serving from twenty after the exile. Many scholars see the Chronicler reflecting the practice of his own day and grounding it in David's authority. Others read David as adjusting the rule of Moses for the larger needs of a permanent temple. Either way, the chapter presents the change as faithful adaptation, not departure.

The work listed is plain and practical: cleaning, storing, baking, measuring. The word for it, avodah, can mean labor, slavery or worship; in the Bible's language, work done for God and the worship of God are not two different things. The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before God each Sabbath. Twice a day the Levites were to stand and give thanks.
passages.later: The law had counted the Levites as ‘men from thirty to fifty years old’ (Numbers 4:3). After the exile, Ezra records that the returned community ‘appointed Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction of the house of the LORD’ (Ezra 3:8).
passages.asks: The Levites' work changed when God's dwelling changed, and the change was faithful, not a loss. Ask what work God may be asking you to set down so that you can take up another. And ask whether you treat the plain tasks of serving, cleaning, setting up, measuring, as worship.
